message.content:
Below is a concise overview of your key rights and protections as a residential tenant in Texas (as of 2026). These rights apply to most private rental agreements—though some may vary slightly depending on local ordinances or special housing programs. | Area | Your Rights (Texas State Law) | Practical Tips | |------|------------------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Keep a copy of the lease, take photos before moving in, and document any pre‑existing damage. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For month‑to‑month leases: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• For fixed‑term leases: landlord must give at least 30 days’ notice if terminating early. | Use certified mail or email with read receipt to prove delivery. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep the premises safe and sanitary. | Report problems promptly in writing; keep copies of all communications. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much rent can increase, but it must be stated in the lease and given proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | Review lease terms carefully; negotiate changes before signing. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 30‑day notice for nonpayment, 10‑day notice for violation of lease).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord files an unlawful detainer action in court. | Respond to notices promptly; consider mediation or legal aid if facing eviction. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlord must give reasonable notice (typically 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of entries; ask for written confirmation of any visits. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Code: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, source of income, etc. | File complaints with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Attorney General if discrimination occurs. | | **Lease Modification** | • Either party can modify the lease in writing, signed by both parties. | Do not sign modifications unless you agree to them; keep copies. | | **Retaliation Protection** | • Landlord cannot retaliate against you for exercising your rights (e.g., reporting code violations). | Document any retaliatory actions; report to HUD or local housing agency. | ### Where to Get Help 1. **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** *Website:* https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection *Phone:* 1‑800‑252‑5290 2. **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** *Website:* https://www.hud.gov/complaint *Phone:* 1‑800‑669‑9777 3. **Local Tenant Associations / Legal Aid Societies** Many cities have nonprofit organizations offering free or low‑cost legal advice and representation. Search “tenant rights” + your city name. 4. **Court‑Ordered Eviction Assistance Programs** Some counties offer mediation services or legal clinics specifically for eviction disputes. --- #### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease - Verify the lease states the exact amount of the security deposit and the conditions for its return. - Confirm the lease specifies the required notice period for termination. - Ensure the lease includes a clause requiring the landlord to maintain habitability standards. - Ask for a copy of the lease in advance of signing so you can review it thoroughly. If you need a sample lease template or help drafting a lease modification, let me know!
